evidence_quotes.quote: The penultimate section of the article deals with the impact of prepaid water meters on Sowetan households, shedding light on the social and personal costs incurred in the process of accessing social citizenship rights.
To ensure cost-recovery and to rid municipalities of the administrative nuisance of overseeing a monthly billing system, the state welcomed the introduction of prepaid water meters.

Against the background of high levels of unemployment and extreme poverty in some areas of South Africa, the City of Johannesburg introduced a Municipal Subsidy Scheme, or what is referred to as an Indigence Policy, which allows people who are too poor to pay for water to register at the city council as ‘indigents’. On the proviso that they accept prepaid meters, their service arrears – which sometimes amount to tens of thousands of Rand – are scrapped.

Interviews with representatives of Johannesburg Water, ward councillors in Soweto and material from other government representatives revealed a belief that the Free Basic Water policy, through the attendant system of prepaid water meters, taught people to use water responsibly and to budget for their water needs.

Several residents started changing their behavioural patterns and were forced to forego certain activities in order to prevent their monthly water consumption from exceeding the amount that was provided for free. For example, most residents cut back on cleaning activities (bathing, dishes and general household cleaning), while some reduce their direct consumption of water for drinking or cooking.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community water service access (and associated sanitation/toilet use) in Soweto and Orange Farm townships, Johannesburg, South Africa.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines municipal and utility water governance, tariff/payment policy, and social movement contestation. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing household water access: (1) cost-recovery tariff and prepayment rules enforced through prepaid water meters versus monthly credit billing above the 6-kilolitre Free Basic Water allocation, (2) eligibility screening, means-testing/home asset inspections, administrative stigma, and conditional debt-relief rules (mandatory acceptance of prepaid meters to write off arrears) under the City of Johannesburg's Municipal Subsidy Scheme (Indigence Policy), and (3) service delivery through corporatised utility Johannesburg Water.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal empirical case study drawing on primary fieldwork interviews conducted in 2006-2007 with Soweto residents, Johannesburg Water management, local ward councillors, and Anti-Privatisation Forum / Social Movements Indaba activists, supplemented by utility manuals, High Court affidavit evidence, and movement documents. Per review rules, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are included even without quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete household access outcomes including automatic supply exhaustion/cut-off after the 6-kilolitre free basic allowance, inability to afford top-up credit, reduced consumption of water for drinking, cooking, bathing, cleaning, and toilet flushing, low water pressure, abandonment of home gardens and micro-enterprises, informal monetised access to drinking water and toilets, and administrative exclusion/stigma under means-tested indigence registration.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (low-income households and residents in Soweto and Orange Farm, Johannesburg, plus utility, municipal, and activist informants; total interview sample size not reported), exposure (prepaid water metering, cost-recovery/Free Basic Water 6 kL cap vs. monthly credit billing, and Indigence Policy means-testing/conditionality), outcome (household water availability, quantity/rationing, affordability trade-offs, continuity, and administrative burden/stigma), and study design (qualitative interview-based socio-legal case study) are all identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative socio-legal case study based on primary interviews (2006-2007) and document analysis
population_and_sample: Low-income township households and residents in Soweto (including Dlamini, Pimville, and Chiawelo) and Orange Farm, Johannesburg, South Africa, alongside interviewed Johannesburg Water officials, local ward councillors, and Anti-Privatisation Forum / Social Movements Indaba activists (interviews conducted in 2006-2007; total N not reported).
exposure: Prepaid water metering and upfront cost-recovery rules above the 6-kilolitre/month Free Basic Water allocation (compared with monthly credit billing) delivered by corporatised utility Johannesburg Water, together with means-testing, home inspections, and mandatory prepaid-meter conditionality for arrears relief under the City of Johannesburg's Municipal Subsidy Scheme (Indigence Policy).
outcome: Household water access, continuity/exhaustion of water supply after the 6 kL free allocation, affordability trade-offs against food and medication, curtailment of drinking, cooking, cleaning, and toilet flushing, low water flow/pressure, informal charges for cups of water and toilet use, and administrative burden/stigma from indigence means-testing (plus community resistance/reconnections).
rationale: This English-language qualitative socio-legal study empirically investigates household water service access in Soweto (and Orange Farm), Johannesburg, South Africa, using primary interviews conducted in 2006-2007 with township residents, Johannesburg Water officials, ward councillors, and Anti-Privatisation Forum activists, alongside documentary and affidavit evidence. It satisfies Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope by analysing upfront cost-recovery/prepayment rules via prepaid water meters above the 6-kilolitre Free Basic Water cap (contrasted with monthly credit billing) and eligibility screening, home-visit means-testing, and conditional debt write-offs under Johannesburg's Indigence Policy. It reports clear household access, quantity/rationing, continuity, affordability, and exclusion outcomes, and qualifies for systematic-review inclusion as a mechanism-relevant qualitative empirical study.
